title: The boat
hookLine: a swimmer swept away in a flood can't save anyone; a skilled boatman can carry many

cards: Every lifeguard learns it early: a drowning person will pull a rescuer under. You don't jump in after someone unless you know what you're doing, because two people in trouble don't make one rescue.

In the Ganges plain, in the rainy season, rivers rose fast and wide, and crossing was a real danger. Everyone knew the difference between a person thrashing in the current and a ferryman standing in a sturdy boat.
The eighth poem of the Sutta Nipata's second chapter builds a whole teaching on that difference.

teach.h: HONOR THE ONE YOU LEARN FROM
teach.b: The poem starts with teachers. Honor the person you learn the truth from, it says, the way the gods honor their king. A teacher who is honored, and pleased, opens up what they know.
A student who listens closely becomes wise and skilled too. Then the warning.

teach.h: A FOLLOWER OF THE CONFUSED STAYS CONFUSED
teach.b: If you follow someone who hasn't understood, a small-minded person who hasn't really grasped it, you'll end up the same: still full of doubt. And then the picture.
Someone falls into a river in flood, the current fast and wide. They're swept along, helpless. How could they carry anyone else across?

teach.h: SWEPT AWAY, OR IN A STRONG BOAT
teach.b: Someone climbs into a strong boat, with oar and rudder. They know the river. They know the method.
That person can carry many others across. The same, the poem says, with someone who truly knows, who has trained and listened deeply and isn't shaken.
They can help others understand, if others are willing to listen. Notice the order of the poem. First you need a good teacher.

Then you need to actually learn. Only then can you carry anyone. It's a gentle warning against rushing to help before you're steady yourself, and it's also a promise: once you are steady, your skill isn't only for you.
The boat holds more than one. In daily life it can look small. A friend who came through a divorce sits with another friend going through one.
A nurse on her tenth night shift talks a new nurse through his first. Each of them knows this stretch of river.

how: Buddhists often describe the teaching as a way of crossing to the far shore, and many communities stress studying with a qualified teacher before teaching others.

o: a ferry fee paid to cross the river
one who has truly learned, able to carry others
a raft to cling to and carry everywhere

games.q: the boat poem: tap the pairs.

s: the poem says anyone can help others across, ready or not
the one swept away in the flood can't carry anyone; first you need to know the river.
the poem begins with honoring the teacher you learn from
as the gods honor their king.
the skilled one in the boat can carry many across

games.q: you see a friend struggling in the same hard season you once got through. what does the boat poem picture as the way to help?
o: jump in, even if you're still struggling too.
help from a steady boat, with what you've truly learned.
wait until they figure it out alone.
games.why: the one in a strong boat, who knows the river and the method, can carry many across; the one swept away can't.

practice: First steady yourself: feet, seat, the breath going in and out, your oar and rudder.
Then think of something you've truly learned to cross, a hard season, a skill, a fear, and of someone still in that river, and let one small thing you know that might help them come to mind.

wordCard.voice: The boat. The poem's picture of someone who has truly learned: steady in a strong boat, with oar and rudder, able to carry many across the flood. Today's word.

orig.note: Pali nava: boat. Sn 2.8 is called the Nava Sutta, the boat discourse.

carryVoice: Your line: take others across. Steady first, and the boat holds more than one. Day five hundred ninety-eight, done.
